title: The One With The Cooking Class

jokes.text: That's no way to sell newspapers. Try, 'Extra! Extra! Read all about it!'
jokes.setup: Someone says 'Hey, I got some bad news' — a straight conversational opener
jokes.punchline: Joey critiques the delivery style as if they're a newsboy, completely ignoring the actual bad news
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey obliviousness — he mishears intent and responds to surface form rather than content. Good character integration because only Joey would do this. Clean structure with a solid subversion of expectation.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown Friend
dialogue.line: I have something to tell you. It's not good news.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown Friend
dialogue.line: But wait, there's more! If you act now, you can get TWO bad things for the price of one!

jokes.text: Two, four, six, one million. Yeah, you got them all.
jokes.setup: Ross announces he ran around and bought all the copies of the Post to hide a bad review from Monica
jokes.punchline: Chandler sarcastically counts 'two, four, six, one million' implying the futility of the plan in a dry, mock-impressed tone
jokes.explanation: Very Chandler — dry wit delivered with economy. The escalation from 'two, four, six' to 'one million' is a well-structured absurdist jump that lands the futility of Ross's plan efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I remember my first good review. It was in the Village Voice back in '92.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: They said I was 'abysmal'.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: But in a good way!

jokes.text: I remember my first good one: 'Everything else in Our Town was terrible. Joey Tribbiani was abysmal.'
jokes.setup: Joey mentions he's had bad reviews, then says he remembers his 'first good one'
jokes.punchline: The 'good review' he recalls is a devastating pan — 'everything was terrible, Joey was abysmal' — but Joey genuinely seems to treasure it because he was singled out
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The setup carefully manufactures the expectation of a good review, then the punchline reveals it's a scathing pan — but Joey's pride in it is entirely consistent with his narcissism and obliviousness. The specific word 'abysmal' (which echoes back later in the episode as a callback) is an inspired word choice. Only Joey Tribbiani could cherish this review. Earns an 8+ because of perfect character integration, tight misdirection structure, and genuine originality in its concept.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God! Oh my God! We're in the newspaper!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: This is so exciting! We're getting press for the restaurant!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Mon, that's not... that's not good press.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What do you mean? It's in the newspaper!

jokes.text: But the good news is, no one in a two-block radius will ever know.
jokes.setup: Monica sees all the newspapers Ross bought and assumes it's because the review is great
jokes.punchline: Chandler drily notes the 'good news' is only localized ignorance — implying the whole city knows
jokes.explanation: Competent Chandler-style dark comedy, sets up the follow-up line well. Not particularly original but functions as a good beat in the sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, look on the bright side. At least the review was limited to just one city.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler, it was in the New York Times.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, but it's only read in New York.

jokes.text: And the rest of Manhattan? They all know.
jokes.setup: Chandler says no one in a two-block radius will know, implying containment
jokes.punchline: Immediately undercuts with 'And the rest of Manhattan? They all know.'
jokes.explanation: Works as a tight two-beat with the previous joke. The rhythm of 'And the rest of Manhattan? They all know.' is punchy and well-economized. Functions as a satisfying button to that mini-sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What about the rest of Manhattan?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, they know.

jokes.text: They say there's no such thing as bad press. You don't think that 'the mahi-mahi was awful-awful' is bad press?
jokes.setup: Someone offers the cliché 'there's no such thing as bad press' as comfort
jokes.punchline: Monica parodies the review's language by mirroring the dish's doubled name 'mahi-mahi' with 'awful-awful,' weaponizing the reviewer's own phrasing
jokes.explanation: Clever wordplay — mirroring 'mahi-mahi' with 'awful-awful' is a genuinely witty construction that takes a well-worn cliché and subverts it with specificity. Shows character (Monica's specificity about food) while also being a genuinely funny linguistic joke.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, there's no such thing as bad press. My mahi-mahi got a review that said it was 'awful-awful.' I mean, at least they rhymed it!

jokes.text: I'm not just saying this because I'm your friend. Your food is abysmal!
jokes.setup: Joey begins reassuring Monica: 'I'm not just saying this because I'm your friend...' — the classic setup for a sincere compliment
jokes.punchline: He delivers a devastating insult instead, apparently thinking brutal honesty IS the supportive friend move — and echoes the exact word from his own beloved bad review
jokes.explanation: The misdirection of 'I'm not just saying this because I'm your friend' perfectly sets up an expected compliment. The pivot to 'Your food is abysmal!' is both a great character moment for Joey (oblivious, tactless) and a callback to his treasured review — the word 'abysmal' now lands doubly because the audience just heard Joey use it fondly. Strong structure and character integration push this near the top tier.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm not just being supportive. I'm being objective.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yes. And I'm telling you, you are a great chef. You just had one bad review.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What did it say?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It said your food was 'inedible.'

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: But look, one person's 'inedible' is another person's... not inedible.

jokes.text: My due date is in one week! / That is seven days.
jokes.setup: Rachel is freaking out that her due date is in one week
jokes.punchline: Ross's response is literally just 'That is seven days' — an utterly useless mathematical restatement
jokes.explanation: Ross's pedantic non-answer is perfectly in character — anxious deflection disguised as precision. The economy is excellent; it's a one-line joke that reveals character while being genuinely funny.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: We need to get a diaper service.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: A diaper service? Rachel, I need to use the bathroom right now.

jokes.text: I had a lot of water. Can we do this after..?
jokes.setup: Rachel is freaking out about the baby, listing things they don't have — Ross is urgently trying to tell her something
jokes.punchline: His urgent thing is that he has to pee — in the middle of a pregnancy crisis conversation
jokes.explanation: Functional bodily humor that also sets up a callback later. Not particularly original but serviceable as a character beat. The 'I had a lot of water' explanation adds a mild extra beat of oversharing.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross, we need to talk about us. I think we should see other people.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? Rachel, no—

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm just kidding! Oh my God, you should see your face right now!

jokes.text: We do not have a diaper service. / Funny you should mention diapers.
jokes.setup: Rachel is listing serious baby necessities; she mentions they don't have a diaper service
jokes.punchline: Ross's 'Funny you should mention diapers' implies he's about to have a bathroom emergency — the word 'diapers' was his cue to exit
jokes.explanation: A decent wordplay/situation joke — the word 'diapers' becomes a double entendre given Ross's bathroom urgency. A bit telegraphed but lands as a mild laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, what if we just all hang out until I meet myself? Then we'll know it's the right time!

jokes.text: Our situation, you know, what we mean to each other... Isn't that weird? / [long pause] Well.. / I'm just kidding. You can go pee.
jokes.setup: Rachel stops Ross with an apparently serious emotional question about their relationship and what they mean to each other — clearly building to a romantic revelation
jokes.punchline: After a long, loaded pause where Ross (and the audience) expects a confession of feelings, Rachel reveals she was just messing with him so he could go pee
jokes.explanation: Smart structure — the scene builds genuine emotional tension around the central Ross/Rachel will-they dynamic, then deflates it with a bathroom callback. The long pause (inferred from 'Well..') is crucial. This also foreshadows the episode's ending beat. Good use of the show's core tension for comedic misdirection.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, you got a job?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's great! How long do you think you'll be able to keep this one?

jokes.text: I've got a job interview. / I thought you already have a job. / And they say you don't pay attention.
jokes.setup: Joey (or another friend) expresses surprise that Chandler has a job interview when he already has a job
jokes.punchline: Chandler's withering 'And they say you don't pay attention' is dripping with sarcasm — it's a compliment that's actually an insult, implying Joey's observation was so basic it barely counts
jokes.explanation: Classic Chandler snark. The sarcastic compliment format is well-worn but executed with his signature cadence. Good character integration — this is specifically Chandler-to-Joey dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm going to cook that critic.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! You can't cook a person, Monica. That's illegal. And delicious.

jokes.text: Wow. How do you know how to do that? / That's what I do now.
jokes.setup: Joey expresses amazement at Chandler's job skills ('data reconfiguration') as if it's a remarkable talent
jokes.punchline: Chandler flatly reveals it's literally his current job — meaning Joey has no idea what his best friend does for a living
jokes.explanation: Plays on the long-running joke that no one knows what Chandler does for a living — most famously exploited in other episodes. The punchline's brevity ('That's what I do now') is perfect deadpan. High character integration because it's specific to both characters' dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I can't believe they're going to put this on the front page!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, Monica, they're not gonna put it on the front page.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Because you're not famous, and nobody cares.

jokes.text: I want to get my revenge. / You cooked him?
jokes.setup: Monica dramatically announces she's getting revenge on the reviewer
jokes.punchline: Joey's first instinct is that she COOKED the man — a darkly absurd leap that makes total sense for a character who thinks with his stomach
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest jokes. 'You cooked him?' is a two-word punchline of near-perfect economy. The dark absurdism of Joey assuming Monica committed culinary cannibalism is both outrageous and entirely consistent with his food-obsessed, non-sequitur-thinking character. The setup is elegant — 'revenge' is an ambiguous word that creates the space for misinterpretation. Earns 8+ for originality, economy, and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm looking for a couch. Something comfortable for two people.

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.line: Are you looking for something for you and your husband?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh no, no. I'm actually going through a really messy breakup right now. My boyfriend—well, ex-boyfriend—he cheated on me with my best friend's roommate. And the thing is, he wasn't even good in bed, so I'm not even sure why I'm upset about it.

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.line: ...I see.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I just need something I can cry on for hours without feeling the springs. Something soft enough for ice cream stains. Do you have anything in that?

jokes.text: I can't wait to read the front page tomorrow: 'Restaurant reviewer admits: I was wrong about Monica.' / The front page? / You really do live in your own little world, don't you?
jokes.setup: Monica grandiosely imagines the newspaper headline she'll generate by making the reviewer eat her soup again
jokes.punchline: Joey's incredulous 'The front page?' followed by 'You really do live in your own little world, don't you?' — especially rich coming from Joey, who is himself deeply delusional
jokes.explanation: The joke has a nice meta-layer: Joey accusing someone of living in their own world is itself ironic given his character. The line 'You really do live in your own little world' is a solid put-down with good rhythm. Elevated by the irony of its speaker.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So anyway, I've been having this really weird thing happen, and I don't know if it's normal, and my gynecologist said—

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, I think this guy doesn't need to know about your gynecologist.

jokes.text: If I'm going to the movie and you're going to the movie, why don't we just go together? How's that for data reconfiguration, huh, Chand?
jokes.setup: Joey and Chandler both independently planned to go to the same movie
jokes.punchline: Joey treats the basic logical deduction of 'go together' as a feat of brilliant problem-solving, using Chandler's impressive-sounding job title as a punchline
jokes.explanation: Joey's self-congratulation on solving a kindergarten-level logic problem as 'data reconfiguration' is a good callback that also illustrates his obliviousness. The nickname 'Chand' adds a nice familial touch. Solid character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross, I can't do this anymore. You're so obsessed with dinosaurs, you named our baby after a Jurassic period fossil.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's not fair! I'm a paleontologist, it's my passion!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Exactly. Your passion is 65 million years old. I need someone whose passion is, you know, current.

jokes.text: Have you ever had two people who weren't wearing crowns spend this much money here?
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel are spending extravagantly at a baby store
jokes.punchline: Ross implies only royalty ('people wearing crowns') would normally spend this much, characterizing their shopping as comically excessive
jokes.explanation: A mild observational joke. The 'crowns' image is an okay metaphor for royalty/wealth but isn't particularly sharp. Gets the point across without much comedic craft.

dialogue.speaker: Sales Woman
dialogue.line: Oh, a paleontologist! That's so impressive!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, he doesn't actually help sick people or anything.

jokes.text: Mr. and Mrs. Geller? / Oh, no, no. / No, no. / We're not married. / We are having a baby but we're not involved...
jokes.setup: The saleswoman assumes Ross and Rachel are a married couple named 'Mr. and Mrs. Geller'
jokes.punchline: Their flustered, over-explained denial spirals into an uncomfortable TMI exposition of their entire relationship history to a stranger
jokes.explanation: Classic cringe comedy — the awkward over-explanation to a stranger is relatable and well-played. The economy suffers slightly because the explanation runs long, but the situation itself is funny and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I have no idea what you guys are talking about.

jokes.text: Or, yes, stranger, we'd like this delivered, please.
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel have been over-explaining their relationship to the saleswoman at length
jokes.punchline: Rachel abruptly cuts off the rambling with a dry 'Or, yes, stranger, we'd like this delivered' — acknowledging the absurdity and snapping back to practical reality
jokes.explanation: The 'Or, yes, stranger' is a perfect button on the cringe sequence. Very economical — the word 'stranger' captures the whole absurdity of what they just did. Rachel's self-aware exasperation is well-characterized.

dialogue.speaker: Saleswoman
dialogue.line: So you're an archaeologist? That's so sexy. You must be like Indiana Jones.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, I don't know about that...

dialogue.speaker: Saleswoman
dialogue.line: Oh come on, the leather jacket, the whip, those biceps...

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I don't really use a whip.

jokes.text: You picked out a lot of dinosaurs. / Yeah. That's one of the reasons why we're not a couple.
jokes.setup: The saleswoman notices Ross picked lots of dinosaur-themed items
jokes.punchline: Rachel confirms the dinosaur obsession is literally a relationship dealbreaker — framing Ross's nerdiness as incompatibility evidence
jokes.explanation: A compact, efficient joke that skewers Ross's paleontology obsession in a character-specific way. Rachel's dry delivery of 'that's one of the reasons' implies a whole list of other reasons, adding comic richness with just a few words.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Indiana Jones? Really? Well, I mean, we do have a lot in common. We're both archaeologists, we both wear leather jackets, we both go on adventures and make incredible discoveries...

jokes.text: I chose those. I'm a paleontologist. / Really? That is so cool. / Don't get too worked up. It sounds like he's a doctor, but he's not.
jokes.setup: Ross defends the dinosaur choices by revealing he's a paleontologist — Katie is impressed
jokes.punchline: Rachel immediately deflates the moment: 'Don't get too worked up. It sounds like he's a doctor, but he's not.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. 'It sounds like he's a doctor, but he's not' is a precisely crafted takedown that perfectly captures the cultural perception of academia vs. medicine, delivered with Rachel's specific mixture of affection and shade. The economy is excellent — it explains the whole joke in one clause. Highly quotable. Earns its high score for structure, economy, and sharp character voice.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross almost got something that wasn't on the list.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You whore!

jokes.text: Standing at a cash register, I'm holding a credit card, and I'm bored.
jokes.setup: Ross and Katie are excitedly bonding over the Walter Alvarez book on paleontology
jokes.punchline: Rachel gives a deadpan status report of her own situation while they talk — highlighting how completely she's been sidelined
jokes.explanation: A good reaction beat that characterizes Rachel's jealousy-before-she-knows-it's-jealousy. The specific detail of 'holding a credit card' — she WANTS to pay, to leave, and yet here she stands — is a nice touch. Economy is high.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, we should alert the church elders! A woman smiled at an unmarried man! Quick, somebody call the Vatican!

jokes.text: That's my gym. / I could tell you work out.
jokes.setup: Katie mentions there's a great gym around the corner from the store
jokes.punchline: Ross says 'That's my gym' and Katie compliments his physique — cutting to Rachel's reaction of watching this flirtation unfold while she's nine months pregnant
jokes.explanation: More of a plot beat than a strong joke — the flirtation escalates the situation but the lines themselves are generic. The comedy is more situational (Rachel watching this happen) than in the dialogue.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I mean, if there was a store called Sluts-R-Us, I wouldn't shop there!

jokes.text: A paleontologist who works out. You're like Indiana Jones.
jokes.setup: Katie has been impressed by Ross's academic credentials and gym membership
jokes.punchline: She compares him to Indiana Jones — a fictional archaeologist — which is both a compliment and a slight (he's a paleontologist, not an archaeologist, and Indiana Jones is fictional)
jokes.explanation: Sets up the running Indiana Jones gag that pays off later. As a standalone joke it's decent — the Indiana Jones comparison is a good pop-culture shorthand that also slightly misidentifies his field, adding a layer of unintentional comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, do they have any openings?

jokes.text: I am like Indiana Jones.
jokes.setup: Katie calls Ross 'like Indiana Jones' as a flirtatious compliment
jokes.punchline: Ross agrees without irony or self-awareness — he fully accepts and believes this characterization of himself
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum comedy. Ross's complete sincerity in accepting the Indiana Jones comparison is perfectly in character with his tendency toward self-aggrandizement. The economy (four words doing all the work) is excellent. Sets up multiple callbacks.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hey Fatty!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Chandler!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What? You are!

jokes.text: A whore. / What? / We were paying, and this saleswoman just started flirting with him.
jokes.setup: Rachel tells Phoebe that Ross 'almost got something that wasn't on the list' at the baby store
jokes.punchline: Phoebe deadpans 'A whore' — an absurdly blunt misinterpretation that reframes the ambiguous phrasing as something scandalous
jokes.explanation: The setup 'Ross almost got something that wasn't on the list' is deliberately vague, and 'A whore' is an unexpected but perfectly logical Phoebe-ism — she's both blunt and oddly non-judgmental about it. Two words carrying enormous comedic weight. The best Phoebe joke in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, when I first met you, you were like, 'Hi, I'm Chandler, I'm funny and I'm—uh—I'm funny and uh—could I BE any more awkward?' And I was like, 'Yes. Yes, you could.'

jokes.text: Oh, my God. Well, the idea.. A woman flirting with a single man? We must alert the church elders.
jokes.setup: Rachel is outraged that a saleswoman flirted with Ross
jokes.punchline: Phoebe mock-panics: 'A woman flirting with a single man? We must alert the church elders.' — highlighting the absurdity of Rachel's outrage with exaggerated mock-alarm
jokes.explanation: 'We must alert the church elders' is a pleasantly odd, specific phrase for mock-alarm — it has a vaguely archaic quality that makes it funnier than a more generic expression would be. Phoebe's role as Rachel's clear-eyed foil is well-deployed here.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I mean, when you first meet Chandler, he seems like kind of a jerk.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What?!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: But then you realize it's just a defense mechanism. He's actually really lonely and desperate for approval.

jokes.text: Here I am, about to pop, and he's out picking up some shopgirl at Sluts-R-Us?
jokes.setup: Rachel is defending her outrage over the flirting saleswoman
jokes.punchline: 'Sluts-R-Us' — a Toys-R-Us parody name that Rachel uses to demean the baby store and its employee in one jealous swoop
jokes.explanation: 'Sluts-R-Us' is a sharp portmanteau insult that's both funny as a wordplay and revealing of Rachel's jealousy. The brand parody is familiar enough to land immediately. Well-characterized as the kind of thing a frustrated, hormonal Rachel would say.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I promise to be completely honest with you. But first, I'm going to run away.

jokes.text: Is that a real place? / Are they hiring?
jokes.setup: Rachel uses the fictional insult 'Sluts-R-Us'
jokes.punchline: Phoebe asks if it's real, then Joey immediately asks if they're hiring — both characters playing their respective absurdist and self-interested notes perfectly
jokes.explanation: A two-beat reaction that perfectly deploys both characters. Phoebe's literal-mindedness ('Is that a real place?') and Joey's self-serving follow-up ('Are they hiring?') is a classic comic escalation that showcases both characters in just seven words. The economy is exceptional — the entire joke is nine words total between two characters.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You know what? Fine. Don't eat it. But if you ever come back here, I'm putting you in the soup.

jokes.text: Hey, Phoebe. Fatty.
jokes.setup: Chandler arrives and greets Phoebe, then Rachel
jokes.punchline: He casually addresses the nine-months-pregnant Rachel as 'Fatty' — with no apparent ill intent, just oblivious affection
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny in context — the pregnancy makes it technically descriptive rather than mean, and Chandler's breezy delivery suggests affection rather than cruelty. But it's not a sophisticated joke; it relies almost entirely on the situational awkwardness.

dialogue.speaker: Food Critic
dialogue.line: Look, I appreciate the gesture, but I can't lie about your soup. It's... it's not good. The broth is oversalted, the vegetables are mushy, and there's a weird aftertaste I can't identify.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: But you have to say it's good! I made it with love!

dialogue.speaker: Food Critic
dialogue.line: That's exactly my problem. I'm a professional. I have integrity. But you're standing there with that knife, and frankly, my integrity doesn't taste as good as I imagine your soup might taste with about six more hours of simmering and completely different ingredients.

jokes.text: I think I know someone who does that. / Me. I do that.
jokes.setup: Chandler explains his interview is for a data reconfiguration job
jokes.punchline: Joey thinks he 'knows someone' who does data reconfiguration — then Chandler has to explain that it's him, Chandler, his best friend/roommate
jokes.explanation: Second beat of the 'nobody knows Chandler's job' running gag. Joey's obliviousness is taken one step further — he doesn't even remember the conversation they just had about this. Well-executed callback that deepens the established joke.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, I really respect that. You know, a man's gotta stick to his principles, even if it costs him.

dialogue.speaker: Critic
dialogue.line: Thank you. I appreciate—

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, yeah, that's great. So, uh, you're gonna leave now, right?

jokes.text: When I first met you, you were like: [pantomimes/describes Chandler's needy behavior] / You don't make a very good first impression.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is warning Chandler that he doesn't make a good first impression before his interview
jokes.punchline: Phoebe reenacts how Chandler came across when she first met him — trying too hard, making nervous jokes, seeming needy
jokes.explanation: Setup for the interview coaching subplot. The joke itself is more of a plot point than a great gag — the actual demonstration isn't visible in the transcript, limiting the analysis. Good character work though.

dialogue.speaker: Cooking Teacher
dialogue.line: That's absolutely right, Monica! You really know your way around a kitchen.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Thank you! I've been cooking for a long time.

dialogue.speaker: Cooking Teacher
dialogue.line: Well, it shows. You know, I have to say, in all my years of teaching, I've rarely seen such natural talent and technique.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wow, that's... that's really nice of you to say.

dialogue.speaker: Cooking Teacher
dialogue.line: I mean it. Have you ever considered cooking professionally? You could really go somewhere with this.

jokes.text: Did you like me when we first met? / Chandler, I'm not gonna lie to you. But I am gonna run away from you.
jokes.setup: Chandler asks vulnerably whether Phoebe liked him when they first met
jokes.punchline: Phoebe starts with 'I'm not gonna lie to you' — implying honesty — then pivots to 'But I am gonna run away from you' — avoiding the honest answer by literally (or figuratively) fleeing
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best-constructed jokes. The structure is elegant: 'I'm not gonna lie to you' sets up an expected brutal honesty, then 'But I am gonna run away from you' subverts it with an escape that is itself honest (she won't lie, she'll just leave). The parallelism of 'I'm not gonna... But I am gonna...' is well-crafted. Highly quotable. Earns 8+ for structure, economy, and originality of the escape maneuver.

dialogue.speaker: Katie
dialogue.line: They forgot an item.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, yeah. It was the only thing left.

jokes.text: She's put on so much weight.
jokes.setup: Phoebe has presumably just run away from Chandler after delivering her punchline
jokes.punchline: Chandler, stung by her exit, comments 'She's put on so much weight' — a catty, petty insult that's his way of saving face after being roasted
jokes.explanation: A quick button joke. Chandler's petty, slightly mean-spirited response to being embarrassed is very in-character. Short and functional — works as a tag on the previous beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh, Katie, that's great! I mean, I would love to go out with you, but I have to be honest — I'm still dealing with some stuff from my last relationship.

dialogue.speaker: Katie
dialogue.line: Oh, okay...

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, no, it's not you! You seem really great. It's just... I'm not in a good place right now.

dialogue.speaker: Katie
dialogue.line: I understand.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: But hey, maybe we could just hang out as friends? You know, get coffee sometime?

dialogue.speaker: Katie
dialogue.line: Sure, that sounds nice.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Great! Although, just so you know, I'm probably going to complain about my love life the entire time.

jokes.text: Either eat it or be in it.
jokes.setup: The reviewer says he doesn't see why he'd put himself through her bouillabaisse again
jokes.punchline: Monica threatens him: 'Either eat it or be in it' — implying she'll cook him if he doesn't comply (a callback to Joey's earlier 'You cooked him?' joke)
jokes.explanation: Six words. One of the most quotable lines in the episode. The dark threat — 'Either eat it or be in it' — works on multiple levels: it's a callback to the 'You cooked him?' joke, it's perfectly menacing without actually making narrative sense, and Monica's intensity makes it feel genuinely threatening. The economy is near-perfect; this could not be said in fewer words. Earns its high score.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, I mean, you're not a bitch. You're just a girl who likes a guy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what? You're kind of a bitch.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, no, you're a total bitch!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You're the biggest bitch I have ever met!

jokes.text: Spoon? [offered after the threat]
jokes.setup: Monica has just threatened to put the reviewer IN her soup if he doesn't eat it
jokes.punchline: She then politely offers him a spoon — the mundane hospitality gesture immediately after a dark threat creates a sharp tonal contrast
jokes.explanation: One word. 'Spoon?' may be the most economical joke in the episode — the entire joke is a single word whose comedy comes entirely from the violent context preceding it. Monica's cheerful pivot from dark threat to polite soup service is a perfect character beat. The abruptness of the transition is what makes it sing. Perfect economy score.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I got my whip. You know, for the, uh... it's just a whip. For whipping. Not for anything else. Just a regular whip that you crack, like Indiana Jones. Very practical tool. Definitely not a... I mean, it's just a whip.

jokes.text: I'm torn between my integrity and my desire to avoid a beating.
jokes.setup: The reviewer is asked what he thinks of the soup after Monica's forceful persuasion
jokes.punchline: He frames his dilemma as a classic moral conflict ('integrity vs. desire to avoid a beating') — treating Monica's soup threat as a genuine physical danger while maintaining his critical posture
jokes.explanation: The reviewer's self-important framing of a ridiculous situation ('my integrity') clashing with the frank admission that he fears Monica is a good comic contrast. 'My desire to avoid a beating' is an unusually blunt phrase for a food critic, which is what makes it funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm not into S&M or anything like that!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I mean, sure, sometimes Rachel likes to be a little rough, and okay, yes, I have a thing for those leather pants she wore that one time, but that's not S&M!

jokes.text: Thattagirl! We should get out of here.
jokes.setup: Monica's soup has been declared 'abysmal' again — her plan has completely failed
jokes.punchline: Joey's cheerful 'Thattagirl!' treats the humiliation as a victory and immediately pivots to practical escape — completely misreading the situation
jokes.explanation: Joey's oblivious encouragement is well-played. 'Thattagirl' in defeat is a classic Joey move — he's supportive without understanding why support might be complicated here.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh wow, so Katie had a successful day at work and asked Ross out? That's great. I'm sure he'll be really happy with his new daddy.

jokes.text: Can anyone tell me the difference between hollandaise and béarnaise sauce? / Well, they both have an egg yolk and butter base. But a béarnaise has shallots, chervil, and most importantly, tarragon. / Very good. What's your name? / [Monica gives her name] / You go to the head of the class!
jokes.setup: Monica and Joey have wandered into an Introduction to Cooking class; the teacher asks a basic question
jokes.punchline: Monica — a professional chef — answers with expert precision, gets praised as a star pupil, completely undermining the revenge plot that brought her here
jokes.explanation: The situational irony of a professional chef being praised at an introduction to cooking class works well. Monica's earnest pride in being told 'you go to the head of the class' is consistent with her competitive character.

jokes.text: This stuff takes up a lot of room. How serious are you about keeping Ben in your life? / My son? Pretty serious.
jokes.setup: Rachel and Ross are dealing with all the new baby stuff that's been delivered
jokes.punchline: Rachel implies Ross may have to choose between his existing son Ben and the new baby's paraphernalia — framed as a dark-humored space problem
jokes.explanation: Dark joke about Ross potentially displacing his son for baby furniture. Ross's straight 'My son? Pretty serious.' response lands well. Not the sharpest joke but has a slight edge to it.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Hello, I'm Regina Phalanges, and I'll be conducting your interview today.

jokes.text: Home deliveries aren't really part of my job description. / Oh, I actually came here to ask you out.
jokes.setup: Katie shows up at Ross's door, ostensibly to deliver a forgotten item
jokes.punchline: She admits the delivery was a pretext — she actually came to ask him out
jokes.explanation: A plot beat more than a great joke. The misdirection is mild and predictable. Functional for story but not comedically distinguished.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Chandler? That's such a cool last name. What's your first name?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's Chandler Bing.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Chandler Bing? Oh my God, that sounds like a stripper name!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, what if I combined them? Bada Bing!

jokes.text: I'm just gonna put this back in my pocket and pretend that didn't happen.
jokes.setup: Ross said 'that sounds great' to Katie's invitation before apparently realizing something (perhaps Rachel is nearby or he's reconsidering)
jokes.punchline: He literally pockets the item and tries to erase the moment from existence — a comically inadequate social maneuver
jokes.explanation: Ross's futile attempt to unring the bell by physically pocketing something is a good visual comedy beat. The literalism of 'putting it back in his pocket' as a way of erasing a social gaffe is funny and in-character.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm not just a number to you, am I?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No, you're also a letter.

jokes.text: I'm free now. You want to get coffee..? / Sure. / Horny bitch. / No, you're a horny bitch! No, you're a horny bitch!
jokes.setup: Ross and Katie are making coffee plans while Rachel is present
jokes.punchline: Rachel mutters 'Horny bitch' at Katie, which sparks an escalating exchange — the insults spiral as Rachel's jealousy erupts into childish name-calling while she's enormously pregnant
jokes.explanation: The escalating 'No, YOU'RE a horny bitch' exchange is gleefully immature and funny, particularly because Rachel is nine months pregnant and supposedly the more dignified party. Broad comedy that works in a live-audience setting.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.line: Did you use cheese in your alfredo?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, I was going to, but then I ate it.

jokes.text: You guys have a good time. I'm just gonna grab my coat. And my whip. / You know, because of Indiana Jones. / Not because I'm into S&M. / I'm not into anything weird, you know? Just normal sex.
jokes.setup: Ross accepts the Indiana Jones comparison sincerely, then tries to make a cool exit with 'I'll grab my coat and my whip'
jokes.punchline: He immediately over-explains to prevent anyone from thinking the whip is for S&M, digging himself deeper with each clarification until he's desperately assuring everyone about his 'normal sex'
jokes.explanation: The Indiana Jones callback pays off beautifully here — Ross's attempt to be cool immediately collapses into anxious over-explanation. The escalation from 'whip' to 'Indiana Jones' to 'not S&M' to 'just normal sex' is a perfect cringe comedy spiral. Very in-character for Ross, who can never let a cool moment rest. Each additional sentence is funnier than the last.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I ate the cheese because I was hungry, okay? It just looked so good sitting there.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And... I also drank the cream.

jokes.text: So you had a good day, huh? Big commission, picked up a daddy.
jokes.setup: Katie/the saleswoman has just left with Ross
jokes.punchline: Phoebe summarizes Katie's day with the blunt assessment 'picked up a daddy' — reducing the flirtation to its most transactional, slightly unflattering terms
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's plain-spoken summation 'picked up a daddy' is characteristically blunt and funny. The phrase 'big commission, picked up a daddy' has a nice rhythm to it. Economy is high.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? I don't know anything about cooking!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I had to ask Rachel how to boil water.

jokes.text: Oh, and it was great to see you too. And you look fantastic. Although you missed a button.
jokes.setup: Katie says a polite farewell; Rachel responds with ostensible warmth
jokes.punchline: Rachel wraps the pleasantry in a passive-aggressive 'you missed a button' — a parting shot disguised as helpfulness
jokes.explanation: Classic passive-aggressive Rachel. The pivot from 'you look fantastic' to the button critique is well-timed and character-specific. Katie's knowing reaction ('Oh, I see what you're doing there') adds a nice layer.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm a very hands-off manager. I don't micromanage, I don't breathe down their necks, I don't check their work every five minutes...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I basically just... show up and collect a paycheck.

jokes.text: Oh, actually, I.. / Oh, okay, I see what you're doing there.
jokes.setup: Rachel points out Katie 'missed a button' — which may or may not be true
jokes.punchline: Katie starts to check, then realizes it's a petty jab and calls Rachel out on it: 'I see what you're doing there'
jokes.explanation: Good beat on the passive-aggressive exchange. Katie calling it out explicitly ('I see what you're doing') is satisfying but doesn't add much beyond confirming what the audience already understood. Functional comic beat.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.line: Why don't you focus on what you do do?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, what?

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.line: What you do do.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Uh, could you use the word 'do' in a sentence?

jokes.text: How long before you have to leave? / An hour. / I can't help you.
jokes.setup: Phoebe offers to help Chandler with his interview prep; he says he has an hour
jokes.punchline: One hour is apparently not enough time to fix Chandler's personality, so Phoebe immediately gives up
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic beat in the exchange. 'I can't help you' delivered after learning he has an entire hour implies the problem is so deep that hours couldn't fix it. Very well-timed and economical.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.line: I have to say, I'm impressed you didn't make a joke about that.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Thank you. It was incredibly difficult.

jokes.text: Hi. Come on in. I'm Regina Phalanges.
jokes.setup: Phoebe volunteers to play the interviewer to help Chandler practice
jokes.punchline: She introduces herself as 'Regina Phalanges' — a fake name that's both absurd and a Phoebe-specific recurring alias (she uses fake names throughout the series)
jokes.explanation: 'Regina Phalanges' is a beloved recurring Phoebe alias in Friends canon — it's hilarious as an absurd fake name (a phalange is an obscure bone/mechanical part) and extremely high in character integration. The name itself is comedy. High quotability because it's a fan-favorite reference in the broader series.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: A star student? I'm going to be a star!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: *wraps herself in aluminum foil*

jokes.text: Chandler Bing. / Oh, Bing. What an unusual name. / You should meet my Uncle Bada.
jokes.setup: Phoebe as 'Regina Phalanges' remarks that 'Bing' is an unusual name
jokes.punchline: Chandler riffs: 'You should meet my Uncle Bada' — 'Bada Bing' being a mob/drum-riff reference
jokes.explanation: A quick, clean wordplay joke — 'Bada Bing' works as both a mob reference (The Sopranos was at peak cultural saturation at this time) and a classic 'ba dum tss' joke-completion sound. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I know everyone hates me, but you know what? I don't care anymore.

jokes.text: I'll let myself out.
jokes.setup: The Uncle Bada joke has apparently fallen flat or been met with silence from Phoebe-as-interviewer
jokes.punchline: Chandler's immediate 'I'll let myself out' — suggesting he's blown the mock interview with the first joke attempt — is a perfect deflated reaction
jokes.explanation: Four words that land perfectly. Chandler's immediate self-awareness that he's just done exactly what Phoebe warned him about — tried too hard with a joke — and his defeated response shows both the problem Phoebe identified and his self-awareness. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I got an A! I got an A! I'm a dork!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yes, you are.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: But I'm a dork who got an A!

jokes.text: Your alfredo's dry. Did you use your cheese? / When you say 'use,' do you mean 'eat as a pre-cooking snack'?
jokes.setup: In the cooking class, Joey's alfredo is dry because he apparently didn't use his cheese
jokes.punchline: Joey has eaten the cheese before it could go into the dish — reframing 'use' as a weirdly precise question since he did 'use' the cheese, just not in the intended way
jokes.explanation: Perfect Joey food joke. The reframing of 'use' — technically he did 'use' the cheese, he ate it — is genuinely clever while remaining completely in character. 'Eat as a pre-cooking snack' has a formal quality that makes it funnier. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm pregnant!

dialogue.speaker: Students
dialogue.line: *gasping*

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.line: With child support payments.

jokes.text: And the cream? / Cheese makes me thirsty.
jokes.setup: Joey ate the cheese; the instructor asks about the cream
jokes.punchline: Joey has also drunk the cream because eating the cheese made him thirsty — the escalation of food consumption is perfectly logical within Joey's food obsession
jokes.explanation: The two-beat escalation is well-constructed: eating the cheese, then drinking the cream because the cheese made him thirsty. The logic is internally consistent within Joey's worldview, which is what elevates it above a simple 'Joey is stupid' joke. 'Cheese makes me thirsty' is a quotable, specific observation.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.line: So you're managing the office now?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's great. I get to tell people what to do all day.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.line: How's that going?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I had to fire someone today.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.line: That's tough.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, I told him he was fired and he just sat there. So I said, 'You can dump your stuff and leave.'

jokes.text: My God! This is amazing! You've never made this before? / Oh, no. I don't know anything about cooking. / I had to ask what it was called when the water makes those bubbles.
jokes.setup: Monica is at a beginner cooking class; the instructor praises her dish
jokes.punchline: Monica plays dumb, claiming total ignorance of cooking — 'I had to ask what it was called when the water makes those bubbles' (i.e., boiling) — while she's a professional chef
jokes.explanation: Monica pretending not to know what 'boiling' is while being a professional chef is a good character-based irony joke. The specific detail — 'the water makes those bubbles' — is an effective way of conveying the absurdity of her false ignorance. Character integration is high.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know, I had the perfect opportunity to make a bathroom joke in that interview, and I didn't take it. I think I'm finally growing up.

jokes.text: Hats off to the chef. / Your mouth was full. I didn't hear. / Hats off to who? / The chef! / That's right!
jokes.setup: The instructor praises Monica, who is pretending to be a beginner
jokes.punchline: Monica forces him to repeat 'the chef' so she can triumphantly confirm it — weaponizing the compliment to remind herself (and presumably the cooking reviewer upstairs) that she IS a great chef
jokes.explanation: Monica's ego needs the specific words 'the chef' — her feigned deafness to extract the validation is very in-character with her competitive nature and wounded pride from the review.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know what? I've been holding this in for way too long. I'm going to say it. That bathroom is... numero dos friendly.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Actually, forget that. Whoever designed this place clearly had some serious... bowel issues.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I mean, the plumbing in here is basically a poop highway.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: This bathroom? Total crap.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Poo.

jokes.text: You'll find that I don't micromanage. I don't shy away from delegating. / That's good to know. But let's stop focusing on what you don't do and focus on what you do do.
jokes.setup: Chandler is listing his management qualities in the real interview
jokes.punchline: The interviewer says 'what you do do' — the double 'do' sounds like 'doo-doo' (excrement), setting up the sustained poop joke that follows
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom wordplay — 'do do' sounding like 'doo-doo.' Not particularly original or sophisticated, but it sets up an escalating sequence that generates genuine laughs. The setup is deliberate and functional.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Coffee? That's what the kids are calling it these days?

jokes.text: What I do do... is create an atmosphere of support. / Nice sidestep on the 'do do' thing. / Hardest thing I've ever done.
jokes.setup: Chandler has been practicing and must respond to 'what you do do' without cracking
jokes.punchline: He successfully navigates past 'do do' in the practice interview; Phoebe praises the sidestep; Chandler admits 'Hardest thing I've ever done'
jokes.explanation: The meta-commentary on the 'do do' sidestep is well-structured — acknowledging the difficulty while maintaining the joke. 'Hardest thing I've ever done' is a good hyperbolic button on the sequence. Character-specific for Chandler (always aware of his own ridiculousness).

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Ross likes Katie? That's so sweet. He's so into her.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, does she like him back?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Because if she doesn't, that's going to be really hard for him. He's so sensitive about rejection.

jokes.text: I mixed the ingredients, I put them in the oven, I took them out. Granted, I should have used the oven mitts, but still.
jokes.setup: Joey proudly presents cookies he made in cooking class
jokes.punchline: His list of accomplishments includes the disclaimer 'I should have used the oven mitts' — implying he burned himself but still counts it as a success because the cookies exist
jokes.explanation: Joey's matter-of-fact mention of burning himself — as a 'granted' aside in his victory speech — is very in-character. The 'but still' that follows is a perfect button that shows his priorities: the cookies happened, the burns are a secondary concern.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Why are you talking to her?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: She's my colleague. We work together.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I don't care. You were smiling at her!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Rachel, she made a joke about the carbon dating machine.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh, so now she's funny too?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, what is going on? You're being completely irrational.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I am not irrational!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Honey, you accused a lamp of flirting with me yesterday.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: That lamp was being very friendly!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You're pregnant, aren't you? It's the hormones.

jokes.text: Monica, my star student. / You called me that before, so I fashioned a star out of foil. / Now, no pressure. If you like my cookies, you give me the star.
jokes.setup: The instructor calls Monica his 'star student'
jokes.punchline: Monica has taken the word 'star' literally and made a physical star from foil, which she now presents as a trophy contingent on cookie approval — exposing her competitive need for validation in an absurdly literal way
jokes.explanation: Monica making a literal foil star for herself is a perfect character joke — it captures her competitive, gold-star-seeking personality in a visual way. The specific detail that she made it out of foil (materials available at a cooking class) adds authenticity. High character integration: this is Monica to her core.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I know I'm being completely unreasonable, but I don't care. I want what I want, and I want it now. Is that so wrong?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm just a selfish person. There, I said it. I'm shallow, I'm vain, and I only think about myself.

jokes.text: Wow, a star! / I know you all hate me, and I'm sorry, but I don't care.
jokes.setup: Monica receives her foil star back after the instructor approves her cookies
jokes.punchline: In her moment of triumph she acknowledges that the other students hate her (for being a ringer in a beginner class) and declares she doesn't care — with the star in hand
jokes.explanation: Monica's unapologetic triumph is very true to character — she knows she's being inappropriate (a professional chef at a beginners' class) but the validation means more than social grace. The honest 'I know you all hate me' acknowledgment followed by 'but I don't care' is a sharp character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh Rachel, I'm so happy for you!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ow! Ow! Get off! You're squishing the baby!

jokes.text: Oh, my God! This is amazing! / You get an A. / I got an A? In school? Hey, I'm a dork!
jokes.setup: Joey's dish gets an A from the instructor
jokes.punchline: Joey's reaction to getting an A — 'I'm a dork!' — reveals that (a) he's never gotten an A before, and (b) he thinks academic achievement = dork, which he now accepts as his identity in this moment of triumph
jokes.explanation: Joey self-labeling as a 'dork' in triumph — because he now associates academic achievement with dorkiness — is a lovely character inversion. His joy is genuine and his self-awareness limited. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, are you serious?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, I'm just kidding. You did it to me earlier.

jokes.text: I think you should give him your star. / Excuse me? / He doesn't know what he's doing. / Nobody knows what they're doing. / I do. I'm a professional chef!
jokes.setup: Joey suggests Monica give him her hard-won foil star
jokes.punchline: Monica's cover is blown — she can't defend her star without revealing she's a professional chef, which undermines her whole beginner-class presence
jokes.explanation: The tension between Monica's cover story and her actual identity comes to a head nicely. The instructor's 'Oh, relax. It's not a courtroom drama' is a funny piece of deadpan that the class applies to Monica's intensity.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I got an A! Can you believe it? I actually got an A in cooking class!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's great, Joe! How'd you manage that?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, let's just say the teacher really appreciated my... hands-on approach.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, please tell me you didn't—

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? I'm just saying I know how to work the system. It's not the first time a teacher's given me an A for extra credit, if you know what I mean.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God.

jokes.text: Oh, relax. It's not a courtroom drama.
jokes.setup: Monica explosively declares 'I do! I'm a professional chef!' in a beginner cooking class
jokes.punchline: The instructor calmly tells her to relax — 'it's not a courtroom drama' — cutting through her intensity with casual understatement
jokes.explanation: The instructor's calm response to Monica's courtroom-dramatic intensity is a good deadpan line. The specific phrase 'courtroom drama' is an unexpected and accurate description of Monica's affect that makes it funnier than a generic 'calm down' would be.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.line: What's the first rule of acting?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Uh... don't act?

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.line: No, it's to know your motivation.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh... yeah, I knew that.

jokes.text: I just got a bad review. / Allessandro's? I love that place! / You do? / You're a great chef. As a person you're a little.. / Oh, I'm crazy, but you liked the food? / Very much.
jokes.setup: Monica reveals she's from Allessandro's, the restaurant that got the bad review
jokes.punchline: A student loves the restaurant, calls Monica a great chef, then carefully implies she's personally difficult ('as a person you're a little...') — Monica cuts him off and prioritizes only the food compliment
jokes.explanation: Monica's immediate parsing of 'great chef but difficult person' — accepting the first, dismissing the second — is perfect character work. Her 'Oh, I'm crazy, but you liked the food?' shows her priorities are entirely about the food, not her personality.

jokes.text: I don't want to go. I'm having fun. / Did either of you pay for this class? / Hey, if my friend says it's time to go, it's time to go!
jokes.setup: Monica and Joey are being asked to leave the class they snuck into
jokes.punchline: Joey, who moments ago wanted to stay, immediately flips his position the moment there's a confrontation — his loyalty to Monica overcomes his desire for cookies
jokes.explanation: Joey's instant reversal from 'I want to stay' to 'if my friend says go, we go' is a sweet character beat that also happens to be funny because of the speed of the pivot. Good loyalty-comedy.

jokes.text: I was the point person on my company's transition from the KL5 to GR6 systems. / You must have had your hands full. / That I did. That I did.
jokes.setup: Chandler is successfully navigating the real interview — sounding competent and calm
jokes.punchline: His 'That I did. That I did.' is both a successful impression of a corporate professional AND a subtle callback to his normal overanxious self being suppressed — the repetition is slightly stilted but he's holding it together
jokes.explanation: Mild comedy — the slight oddness of 'That I did. That I did.' suggests Chandler is doing his best impression of a smooth professional and it's slightly off. More of a tonal beat than a full joke.

jokes.text: So let's talk a little bit about your duties. / My duties?
jokes.setup: The interviewer uses the word 'duties' in a professional context
jokes.punchline: Chandler's reaction — 'My duties?' with barely suppressed panic — signals that he's hearing 'doo-doo-ies' and barely holding it together
jokes.explanation: Callback to the 'do do' rehearsal joke — now deployed in the real interview. Chandler's echo of 'My duties?' is the first crack in his composure. Functional but the joke exists mainly to set up the later payoff.

jokes.text: You'll be heading a whole division, so you'll have a lot of duties. / I see. / But there'll be 30 people under you, so you can dump a certain amount on them.
jokes.setup: The interviewer is explaining Chandler's responsibilities using 'duties' repeatedly
jokes.punchline: 'You can dump a certain amount on them' — 'dump' compounds the doo-doo imagery, escalating the accidental scatological language while remaining professionally appropriate
jokes.explanation: The addition of 'dump' to the 'duties' escalation is well-timed. The interviewer is completely unaware, which makes Chandler's internal struggle funnier. The joke has built momentum across three beats now.

jokes.text: I was really nervous. I'm told I come on too strongly. And then it was really hard to sidestep that 'duty' thing. / Duties? / Doodies? / Poo?
jokes.setup: The interview is apparently over; Chandler lets his guard down and mentions the 'duty' issue
jokes.punchline: The interviewer, now confused, tries to follow Chandler's regression: 'Duties? Doodies? Poo?' — the descent from professional vocabulary to baby talk is a perfect escalating de-evolution
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the entire 'duties' running gag. 'Duties? Doodies? Poo?' is a brilliantly structured three-step devolution from formal to infantile, with the interviewer himself doing the translation. Each step down the ladder is funnier than the last. The interviewer's bewildered participation in Chandler's private poop-word crisis is a perfect comedic culmination. This is the episode's biggest laugh moment — high impact, perfectly structured escalation. Earns 8+ for structure, escalation craft, and the sheer joy of the payoff.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. This doesn't count. Okay? The interview was over. / That was the real Chandler Bing. This is some crazy guy. / Call security! There's a crazy guy out in the hall!
jokes.setup: Chandler has completely blown the post-interview moment and is now desperately trying to reclaim his professional image
jokes.punchline: He shifts from claiming the outburst was 'some crazy guy,' to then calling security on himself — a spiral of self-contradiction that gets worse with each attempt to fix it
jokes.explanation: Chandler's attempts at damage control — 'that was some crazy guy,' followed by 'call security on that crazy guy' (himself) — is a great escalating self-destruction. The logic of the joke is perfect: each fix makes it worse. 'Call security! There's a crazy guy out in the hall!' is very quotable.

jokes.text: Poo? / I'll look forward to your call.
jokes.setup: Chandler has been spiraling; the interviewer is presumably trying to close professionally
jokes.punchline: Chandler's final 'Poo?' — still fixated on the word — followed by the interviewer's magnificently deadpan 'I'll look forward to your call' as if everything is normal
jokes.explanation: The interviewer's 'I'll look forward to your call' as a straight button to Chandler saying 'Poo?' one more time is a near-perfect button. The interviewer's professionalism in the face of Chandler's breakdown is funnier than any outraged response would be. The juxtaposition — 'Poo?' / 'I'll look forward to your call' — is excellent comic structure. The economy of using five words to close a sustained comedic sequence earns its high score.

jokes.text: It was fun. We just had coffee. / Oh, uh-huh, uh-huh, coffee, a little rub-rub-rub under the table?
jokes.setup: Ross reports back that his date with Katie was just coffee
jokes.punchline: Rachel's mock-casual interrogation 'uh-huh, uh-huh, coffee, a little rub-rub-rub under the table?' — the childish 'rub-rub-rub' exposing her jealousy through an absurdly specific and silly accusation
jokes.explanation: The 'uh-huh, uh-huh' mock-casual setup followed by the specific, ridiculous 'rub-rub-rub' — delivered as if that's the standard suspicious move — is funny because of its silliness. It reveals Rachel's jealousy while making her look slightly unhinged in a charming way.

jokes.text: No. No, she was nice. I mean, she was a little slutty, but who isn't?
jokes.setup: Ross asks if Rachel doesn't like Katie
jokes.punchline: 'She was a little slutty, but who isn't?' — the rhetorical question normalizes the supposed sluttiness, making it both a dismissal of Rachel's own insult and a weirdly philosophical acceptance
jokes.explanation: The turn from 'she was a little slutty' to 'but who isn't?' is a surprisingly smart move — the universal qualifier ('who isn't?') both undercuts the insult and reveals Rachel's self-awareness about her own hypocrisy. The economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Of course you did. You'd date a gorilla if it called you Indiana Jones.
jokes.setup: Ross says he liked Katie
jokes.punchline: Rachel's 'You'd date a gorilla if it called you Indiana Jones' — using the Indiana Jones callback to devastatingly skewer Ross's vanity and gullibility
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The specificity of 'a gorilla' (not just 'anyone') and the Indiana Jones callback creates a perfectly constructed insult that reveals exactly why Ross fell for the flirtation. It's precise, funny, and highly quotable. 'You'd date a gorilla if it called you Indiana Jones' is a line that could stand alone as a great comedy insult. High on structure, economy, character integration, and originality.

jokes.text: Did you get a fresh batch of pregnancy hormones today?
jokes.setup: Rachel has been unusually territorial and jealous about Ross's date
jokes.punchline: Ross's 'Did you get a fresh batch of pregnancy hormones today?' frames her jealousy as medically explainable — both deflecting and gently calling her out
jokes.explanation: A solid line — 'a fresh batch of pregnancy hormones' has a clinical specificity that makes it funnier than 'are you being hormonal.' The word 'batch' (as if they're delivered in quantities) adds an absurdist tinge.

jokes.text: I want you to be at my constant beck and call, 24 hours a day. / I'm very sorry, but that is just the way that I feel.
jokes.setup: Rachel is confessing her unreasonable jealousy to Ross
jokes.punchline: She openly admits she wants him at her 'constant beck and call, 24 hours a day' — framing an outrageously unreasonable demand with an apologetic delivery that makes it simultaneously endearing and funny
jokes.explanation: Rachel's honest, apologetic delivery of an absurd demand is very character-specific. The 'I'm very sorry, but that is just the way that I feel' is both self-aware and completely unapologetic. Decent character comedy.

jokes.text: True, but you're allowed to be unreasonable. You're having our baby.
jokes.setup: Rachel acknowledges she's being unreasonable in demanding Ross's total devotion
jokes.punchline: Ross agrees she's unreasonable but grants the unreasonableness as a pregnancy privilege — a loving but slightly absurd logical concession
jokes.explanation: Sweet and functional. 'You're allowed to be unreasonable. You're having our baby.' is a reasonable line for Ross that also has gentle comedy in its matter-of-fact acceptance of her irrationality.

jokes.text: You feel better? / No, not really. You're pressing the baby into my bladder and now I have to pee.
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel have shared a tender hug
jokes.punchline: Rachel's response to 'do you feel better?' is 'no — you're pressing the baby into my bladder' — the romantic moment physically deflated by pregnancy's unglamorous reality, and a callback to the bladder/bathroom thread from the beginning
jokes.explanation: A nice structural mirror — the episode opened with Ross needing to pee and now closes a romantic scene with Rachel needing to pee. The deflation of the tender moment by physical reality is a good comedic beat.

jokes.text: Oh, Rach, I was just messing around. / Like you did when I had to pee? / Oh! I knew that. I knew that! I was just messing with you too!
jokes.setup: Rachel seems to respond emotionally to Ross's 'do you want something more?' — then Ross says he was just messing
jokes.punchline: Rachel immediately calls back to the pee scene from the beginning — 'like you did when I had to pee?' — reversing the power dynamic; then Ross hilariously insists he 'knew' she was messing and claims he was messing too, clearly lying
jokes.explanation: The final scene's comedic payoff is structurally elegant: Rachel uses Ross's own 'pee misdirection' move from the opening act against him, and his panicked 'I knew that! I was just messing with you too!' is a classic Ross over-correction that reveals he absolutely did mean it. The callback bookends the episode beautifully and reveals real character through the comedy. High structure and character integration earn 8+.

jokes.text: Okay. Because for a minute you seemed.. / No, it's just.. / Like you actually.. / That's just because I'm such a good messer!
jokes.setup: Rachel probes whether Ross actually meant it; both characters dance around stating the obvious
jokes.punchline: Ross's desperate 'That's just because I'm such a good messer!' — a transparently ridiculous claim that he's skilled at pretending to have feelings
jokes.explanation: 'I'm such a good messer' is a great Ross line — the pride he takes in his supposed deception skill, which is entirely unconvincing, is perfectly character-specific. The interrupted exchanges leading up to it ('For a minute you seemed.. / No, it's just.. / Like you actually..') build the cringe tension well.

jokes.text: I had a great time. I learned how to bake, ate great food. It's my first A since 7th grade and I didn't even sleep with the teacher.
jokes.setup: Joey is reflecting happily on the cooking class experience
jokes.punchline: 'It's my first A since 7th grade and I didn't even sleep with the teacher' — the casual implication that he DID sleep with teachers to get A's in 7th grade is delivered as a point of pride in his current achievement
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. The implication that Joey slept his way to a 7th grade A is both dark and completely believable for his character. The pride — 'and I didn't even sleep with the teacher' — frames the absence of sexual manipulation as an accomplishment, which is a perfect Joey worldview. The economy is excellent; a single clause does enormous comedic work. High character integration because only Joey's history and mindset would make this joke work.

jokes.text: Oh, look. Acting for Beginners. / Yeah. / Wanna feel good about yourself? / What the hell!
jokes.setup: Joey and Monica pass by another class — 'Acting for Beginners'
jokes.punchline: Joey suggests they attend to feel good about themselves — a supremely confident actor suggesting he'll dominate a beginners' acting class the way Monica dominated the cooking class
jokes.explanation: A good setup for the final joke. The parallel to the cooking class situation, now reversed (Joey is the professional), creates anticipation for the ending punchline. Monica's 'What the hell!' is an enthusiastic acceptance.

jokes.text: Let's start with some basics. Can anybody tell me what the difference between upstage and downstage is? / [Joey raises hand, presumably] / [Cut to end of class] / Yeah, this was a stupid idea.
jokes.setup: Joey confidently enters the acting class expecting to dominate, as Monica dominated the cooking class
jokes.punchline: The final scene shows Joey and Monica sitting at the end of class with Monica saying 'this was a stupid idea' — implying Joey was actually terrible or no better than the beginners, completely subverting the expectation his confidence built
jokes.explanation: The final joke of the episode lands well because it inverts the cooking class sequence: Monica dominated hers, Joey presumably failed his. 'Yeah, this was a stupid idea' is a great button — delivered by Monica, who was in this same position earlier. The structural symmetry makes it satisfying as a closing joke.

tmdb_overview: Monica's restaurant gets a bad review in the Post. After confronting the critic who wrote it, she decides to join a cooking class, with Joey in tow. Meanwhile, Rachel gets jealous when Ross hits it off with a woman at the baby department store. And Chandler prepares for a job interview after Phoebe tells him that he makes a bad first impression.
insight: Mid-season slump: below-average density and impact, leaning on cringe over laughs.
